extracted.intended_audience: state air agencies, EPA regional staff, owners/operators of electric generating units (EGUs), utilities, RTOs/ISOs, PUCs, and other stakeholders participating in state plan development under CAA section 111(d)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for preparing, submitting, and revising state plans implementing the EPA's emission guidelines for affected EGUs under CAA section 111(d), including reporting by EGUs, coordination with reliability authorities, timelines, EPA review processes, and related permitting implications (NSR/BACT/NNSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: EGU deactivation reporting and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an EGU intends to permanently cease operation, operators must provide an initial notice to the relevant reliability authority of the deactivation date and submit an official retirement filing (or equivalent). Supporting regulatory documents must be provided, including correspondence and official filings with RTOs/ISOs/balancing authorities/PUCs or other applicable authorities; any deactivation-related reliability assessments; filings with the SEC or investor notices (e.g., references in 10-K/10-Q) mentioning the EGU's plans; integrated resource plans and PUC orders referring to or approving the deactivation; reliability analyses by RTO/ISO/reliability authorities; notifications that the EGU may be needed for reliability notwithstanding intent to deactivate; and any notifications altering the timing of deactivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators must include documentary evidence from relevant authorities and filings showing deactivation plans and any reliability-related communications or changes. For each remaining year prior to permanent cessation, operators must submit an annual status report to the EPA that includes: (1) progress on each process step identified in the initial report; (2) supporting regulatory documents and correspondence demonstrating progress; and (3) regulatory documents and SEC filings issued since the prior report. EGUs that cease operation by Jan 1, 2032 must submit a final report within 6 months of their committed closure date documenting actions taken post-cessation to ensure permanence (including regulatory filings or decommissioning plans).

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan submission deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: States must submit their CAA section 111(d) state plans to the EPA 24 months after publication of the final emission guidelines in the Federal Register (superseding subpart Ba's default 18-month timeline for this rulemaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA chose 24 months to accommodate required coordination among states, owners/operators, and reliability authorities given the complexity of the source category. The Agency found 24 months adequate given reductions in scope from the proposal (fewer affected EGUs, fewer subcategories, exemption of certain units). Comments requesting longer timeframes (e.g., 36 months) were considered but not adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination with reliability authorities and meaningful engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: State plan development must include substantial consultation and coordination among state air agencies, ISOs/RTOs/balancing authorities, PUCs, owners/operators of affected EGUs, and other pertinent stakeholders to ensure plans accommodate reliability, regulatory, and other overlapping considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should integrate decision-making across agencies and use EPA-provided information and tools to inform meaningful engagement strategies. Meaningful engagement may include identifying pertinent stakeholder communities, using facility-specific emissions information and CCS emission implications, and leveraging existing state tools/programs. EPA expects consultation to be ongoing during plan development. Examples of enhanced engagement (applicable in permitting contexts) include extending comment periods, holding multiple public meetings, and providing translation services for LEP communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for pre-submission studies (feasibility vs FEED)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA expects that, as part of state planning, some preliminary steps such as an initial feasibility study are typical; however, EPA does not assume owners/operators will undertake FEED studies or other major implementation steps prior to state plan submission absent a state law requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility studies are considered a reasonable preliminary assessment before committing to a specific control technology. EPA explicitly does not base compliance deadlines on an assumption that owners/operators will have completed FEED or similar significant steps before state plan adoption/submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan content: assignment of EGUs to subcategories and legal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: States must assign each affected EGU to an appropriate subcategory in their state plan and have in place all legal instruments necessary to implement the requirements for that subcategory by the time of state plan submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because BSERs for coal-fired units can require long lead times, assignment provides regulatory certainty and is generally binding unless the state submits an approved plan revision. States should ensure plans clearly identify subcategory assignments and include enforceable mechanisms (regulatory, statutory, contractual) to implement standards of performance by the applicable timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-path/multi-path standards approach disallowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is not finalizing an approach that would allow coal-fired steam generating units to have two (dual-path) or multiple standards of performance submitted to EPA in a state plan based on potential inclusion in different subcategories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the final rule contains only two coal-fired subcategories (not the previously-proposed structure where dual-path could be realistic), states must pick the subcategory for each affected EGU in the initial plan. If an affected EGU wishes to change subcategories later, the state must submit a plan revision sufficiently in advance of the new subcategory's compliance date to permit EPA review and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan revisions: process, requirements, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: State plan revisions are permitted but are generally subject to the same submission requirements as initial plans (including meaningful engagement and subpart Ba implementing regulations). Approved components of an initial state plan remain federally enforceable until EPA approves a superseding revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is not establishing a cutoff moratorium date for revisions prior to the first compliance date, but cautions that plan revisions submitted too close to the first compliance date (e.g., after Nov 1, 2028 for a Jan 1, 2030 compliance date, given EPA's review time) may not allow sufficient time for EPA approval. States and affected EGUs should plan to avoid noncompliance by timing revisions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA review timelines and possible actions on state plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Under revised subpart Ba, EPA must determine completeness of a state plan submission within 60 days of receipt. Once a submission is deemed complete, EPA must take final action on the state plan within 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA fails to make a completeness determination within 60 days, the submission is deemed complete by operation of law as of that date. Upon review, the Administrator may fully approve, fully disapprove, partially approve/partially disapprove, or conditionally approve a state plan submission. Any components EPA approves become federally enforceable. EPA will review plans for 'satisfactory' compliance with applicable requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic extension of compliance dates if EPA misses review deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will not provide automatic extensions of state plan compliance dates simply because the Agency fails to meet the 12‑month deadline for action on a plan submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explained that making compliance dates contingent on EPA's action date would create regulatory uncertainty and uneven application of requirements across states. States and sources should therefore plan based on the statutorily and regulation‑specified compliance dates, not on potential EPA delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal plan triggers and promulgation timing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's obligation to promulgate a Federal plan (under subpart Ba) is triggered where: (1) a state does not submit a plan by the submission deadline; (2) EPA determines a submission does not meet completeness criteria and the statutory time period for state submission has elapsed; or (3) EPA fully or partially disapproves a state's plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a state fails to submit a plan by the deadline, subpart Ba gives EPA 12 months from the state plan submission due date to promulgate a Federal plan; other triggers shift the 12‑month clock accordingly (e.g., from the date of disapproval). For the final emission guidelines, if a state fails to submit by the 24‑month deadline, EPA would have an obligation to promulgate a Federal plan within 36 months of publication of the final guidelines (earliest possible obligation). Before promulgation of a Federal plan, EPA must conduct meaningful engagement with pertinent stakeholders. Upon application by an owner/operator, EPA may provide a less‑stringent standard or longer compliance schedule (RULOF process) consistent with subpart Ba procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSR permitting applicability and program distinctions (major/minor/PSD/NNSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Source Review (NSR) program applies to new construction and modifications: major NSR (including PSD for attainment/unclassifiable areas and NNSR for nonattainment areas) applies to sources meeting major thresholds; minor NSR applies to smaller projects that do not meet those thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States have primary responsibility for issuing NSR permits and may customize programs within EPA regulation limits (40 CFR 51.160–51.166). If a state lacks EPA‑approved authority, EPA issues or delegates permits under cited CFR sections. Major NSR requirements depend on the area's air quality designation for each pollutant at permit time. Minor NSR has more permitting flexibility and no statutory minimum control technology requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: NNSR offsets and alternatives analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources seeking Nonattainment NSR (NNSR) permits must provide or purchase emission offsets to compensate for increases from the new source or modification and must perform an analysis of alternatives as required by CAA 173(a)(5) and implementing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offsets are decreases in emissions that compensate for increases from the proposed source/modification. Where PSD permitting methods are insufficient to ensure NAAQS protection, applicants may undertake mitigation measures analogous to offsets. The regulations require an alternatives analysis; see 40 CFR 51.165(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation and environmental justice considerations in NSR/PSD permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting authorities must provide opportunity for public hearings and written/oral comment on air quality impacts, alternatives, control technology, and other appropriate considerations (per CAA 165(a)(2) and 40 CFR 51.166(q)(2)(v)). Environmental justice (EJ) concerns may be considered in permit decisions and via enhanced public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA/EAB guidance indicates that permitting authorities can examine plausible claims of disproportionate impacts and may conduct freestanding EJ analyses for PSD permits. The 'alternatives' and 'other appropriate considerations' language can be interpreted to allow incorporation of siting and EJ concerns raised in public comments, potentially resulting in permit conditions based on those considerations. Permitting authorities may enhance participation (extend comment periods, hold multiple meetings, provide translation) and can take informal steps to engage communities earlier in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT determination criteria and the EPA recommended five‑step 'top‑down' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: For PSD (major NSR) permits, permitting authorities must establish emission limitations reflecting Best Available Control Technology (BACT) for each pollutant subject to PSD. BACT is assessed case‑by‑case considering emission reductions each control would achieve and the associated energy, environmental, economic, and other costs. BACT cannot be less stringent than any applicable NSPS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many permitting authorities apply EPA's five‑step 'top‑down' approach: (1) identify all available control options with potential practical application for the regulated pollutant and emissions unit; (2) evaluate and eliminate options that are technically infeasible; (3) rank remaining options from most to least effective; (4) evaluate energy, environmental, economic, and other impacts/costs of options; (5) eliminate options not achievable based on those considerations from the top down and select the most effective remaining option as BACT. The BACT review need not include inherently lower‑polluting processes that would fundamentally redefine the source's purpose, although permitting authorities have discretion to consider broader options and may do so if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT vs. NSPS and variation across permitting contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: BACT determinations for NSR permits may differ from control requirements established by NSPS or emission guidelines under CAA section 111; a source's permit BACT requirement could therefore be more or less stringent than the applicable section 111 standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities must ensure BACT is not less stringent than any NSPS. Because statutory/regulatory bases differ for NSR control tech reviews versus NSPS/emission guideline standards, states and applicants should expect potential differences in applicable control requirements depending on the program and permit.
